FDA News Release

FDA Approves First Treatment for Limb-Girdle Muscular Dystrophy Type 2I/R9

More Press Announcements

For Immediate Release:
November 23, 2026

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today approved Welgemda (ribitol), the first medicine for treating limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2I/R9 (LGMD2I/R9), a rare inherited muscle disease, for adults and pediatric patients weighing at least 30 kg. Welgemda is the first therapy approved for any form of limb-girdle muscular dystrophy.

“Today’s approval is a historic milestone for patients and families living with limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, delivering the first-ever FDA-approved treatment for this disease, backed by clinical evidence,” said Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, J.D. “Under the Trump Administration’s commitment to accelerating innovation and removing unnecessary barriers for rare disease therapies, while maintaining high standards for safety, the FDA is proud to deliver real hope and meaningful progress for patients who have waited far too long for options.”

LGMD2I/R9 is caused by mutations in the FKRP gene, which disrupt a key biological process in muscle cells. In healthy individuals, the FKRP enzyme helps attach sugar molecules to a protein called alpha-dystroglycan, which acts as an anchor, helping muscle cells connect to surrounding tissue. When this process is disrupted, muscle cells become fragile and break down over time, leading to progressive weakness, difficulty walking, and in many patients, impaired breathing. Symptoms typically appear in childhood or early adulthood and worsen over time.

“Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy is a progressive muscle disease that gradually takes away a patient’s ability to walk, breathe, and live independently, often beginning in childhood,” said Laura Jawidzik, M.D., Director of the Division of Neurology 2 in the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research. “The clinical data supporting Welgemda's approval show meaningful improvements in walking speed and lung function, and we are encouraged by what that can mean for patients' daily lives.”

The precise mechanism of Welgemda in the treatment of LGMD2I/R9 is not fully known, but may involve increases in a natural sugar molecule (matriglycan) that anchors alpha-dystroglycan in muscle tissue. The medicine is taken as an oral solution twice daily, mixed with water.

Welgemda was evaluated in a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind study (NCT05775848) involving 112 patients with genetically confirmed LGMD2I/R9. Patients were randomly assigned to receive either Welgemda or placebo for up to 36 months. At a planned interim analysis after 12 months of treatment, patients receiving Welgemda showed significant improvements in two key measures compared to those receiving placebo. Specifically, patients showed improvements in walking speed, measured by the 100-meter timed test, and lung function, measured by forced vital capacity (an indicator of respiratory muscle health). Patients treated with Welgemda also showed significant increases in glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan, indicating the drug was reaching its intended target at the proposed dose. The most common adverse reactions were gastrointestinal effects (e.g., diarrhea, stomach pain) and joint pain.

Welgemda received Orphan Drug, Fast Track, and rare pediatric disease designations for the treatment of LGMD2I/R9. Welgemda is manufactured by ML Bio Solutions Inc. and distributed by BridgeBio Pharma, Inc.
